title: What More Than 150,000 Phone Calls Taught Us About Running a Dental Practice
html:
Written by: Nate Jeal, DMD

Most dentists have a good sense of what’s happening in their practice. They feel like the phones are being answered, that new patients are coming in, and that the schedule is full enough.

But feeling and knowing are different things.

After analyzing more than 150,000 inbound calls across hundreds of dental practices, I can tell you that the gap between what practice owners believe is happening and what the data actually shows may be the single biggest blind spot in dentistry.

The Front Door Problem Nobody Measured

Every dental practice has a physical front door, but the phone is an equally important entry point. Before a patient sits in your chair or experiences your clinical work, they call. And in those 2 or 3 minutes, they decide whether your practice is the one.

Until recently, it wasn’t really possible to measure what happened in those few minutes. The phone rang. Someone answered, or they didn’t. If they didn’t, the patient called somewhere else, and it never showed up in any report. If the call was answered, nobody evaluated whether the conversation turned the caller into a booked appointment or let them slip away.

The data didn’t exist.

And the phone is only part of it. A patient who fills out a form after seeing an ad or visiting your website is standing at that same front door, at the same vulnerable moment, deciding whether anyone will respond before they move on. Most practices can’t respond fast enough, so the patient the practice paid to generate cools off and schedules somewhere else. The front door isn’t just the phone ringing. It’s every moment a patient reaches out, on any channel, at the instant their intent is highest.

What we found is that understanding the conversation matters as much as the conversion. When you study the intent behind every inbound conversation across hundreds of practices, patterns emerge that no single practice could ever see on its own.

Demand Intelligence: Reading What Your Phones are Telling You

We now classify every interaction by intent. Was it a new patient trying to book? An existing patient confirming? Someone requesting a records transfer to another practice? A billing question, or a cancellation? Each one tells you something different about the health of the practice.

New patient call volume tells you whether demand is strong enough to grow, or barely enough to hold steady. The gap between callers who wanted to book and appointments actually booked tells you how much production is disappearing in the conversation itself. Across our network, that gap is larger than most owners would be comfortable knowing, and often the reason behind it is the part that matters most. Appointment availability. Insurance participation. Fees. Any one of these can affect conversion as much as answering the call in the first place.

Records transfer requests are the metric nobody tracks and every owner should. Each one is a patient leaving. Not thinking about leaving. Like, actually leaving. When that number starts climbing, something in the practice needs attention, and most owners never see it, because it’s buried in calls nobody categorizes.

Cancellation patterns tell you whether your schedule is stable or falling apart, and whether there are controls in place at the time of scheduling. A high cancellation rate isn’t a scheduling inconvenience. It’s a diagnostic signal about patient commitment, or about friction somewhere in the experience.

Without good data, practices make million-dollar decisions on a feeling that things are fine.

Adding the Economics Layer

Knowing who is calling and what they want is the demand side. But demand without economics is only half the picture.

A new patient calling to book a cleaning has a different lifetime value than one calling about a specific treatment. A PPO practice runs on different margins than a fee-for-service one. Understanding what a new patient is worth is a math problem, but serving them well enough to realize that value means knowing their insurance, their coverage, and where your fees sit against their plan. Pulling a complete benefit breakdown from the carrier is well within reach of the best agents now—annual maximums, deductibles, coverage percentages, frequency limits, usage. The full picture, verified at the source.

The average front desk spends hours every week on hold with carriers, gathering that information one call at a time. That time goes back to the team so that they can focus on the patients standing right in front of them.

Link the demand data from inbound conversations to the insurance and financial profile of the patients behind them, and you get something no dental practice has ever really had: a live view of what your growth is actually worth.

Put those pieces together, and you have something new. A system that captures demand the moment it arrives, on any channel, answers the patient’s questions, books the appointment, and validates the insurance in real time, sharing it back to the practice. It automates the front end of patient acquisition across voice and text, and confirms the economics before the patient ever walks in. Overhead shrinks, and capacity grows, without adding a single person to the front desk.

From Feeling to Facts

Conventional practice management approaches rely on intuition and trailing indicators. Production reports tell you what happened last month. They don’t tell you what’s happening right now on your phone lines, in your schedule, or in the gap between a patient’s interest and their commitment. Agents can show you the parts of the business that have always been invisible. The calls that went to voicemail. The new patients who hung up. The insurance data locked behind long holds. The signals buried in conversations nobody was listening to.

The patterns are clear, and dentists who can see them are positioned to make better decisions than those still guessing.

The question isn’t whether your clinical skills are good enough. Of course they are. The question is whether you know what’s happening at the front door of your business. After studying more than 150,000 calls, I can tell you most practices don’t. Not because they don’t care, but because until recently there hasn’t been a reliable way to access the information. That’s what we are here to fix.
